title: etcd, killed by its own health check
role: You run a free online lab platform on a single-master kubeadm cluster: one cloud VM, with etcd running as a static pod.

source.label: Matt Oswalt: December 4 NRE Labs outage post-mortem (2018)

brief: Tuesday morning: lessons won't load. On the master, `kubectl` says `The connection to the server 203.0.113.10:6443 was refused`.

steps.situation: The API server doesn't answer. What first?

choices.text: Look at all containers on the master, including exited ones, and the kubelet log
choices.why: With the API down, `kubectl` can't tell you anything. The container runtime and the kubelet can.
It did bring `kubectl` back for a while in the real outage. Then it broke again, and you know no more than before.
Destroying the evidence before you know the cause. The real rebuild took about 30 minutes and the fault came straight back.

steps.situation: A teammate restarted the kubelet, `kubectl` worked, and they tweeted that the outage was fixed. Ten minutes later lessons fail again.
steps.evidence:
$ kubectl -n kube-system get pods
NAME                       READY  STATUS   RESTARTS
etcd-master                1/1    Running  183
kube-apiserver-master      1/1    Running  183
kube-controller-manager    1/1    Running  91

choices.text: Post one honest update: still broken, investigating, next update in 30 minutes
choices.why: Correcting a premature "resolved" quickly keeps users' trust. A status or maintenance page saves you answering each one.

choices.text: Say nothing until it's really fixed
choices.why: Users who read "fixed" and see failures assume you don't know.

choices.text: Look only at STATUS: everything is Running
choices.why: The restart counts are the story: 183 restarts of etcd and the API server.

steps.evidence:
$ sudo docker ps -a --filter name=k8s_etcd --format '{{.Status}}' | head -3
Up About a minute
Exited (0) 2 minutes ago
Exited (0) 4 minutes ago
$ sudo journalctl -u kubelet | grep -i etcd | tail -1
... Liveness probe failed ... container etcd ... will be restarted

choices.text: Each etcd lives under two minutes and exits cleanly: check what is killing it
choices.why: A clean exit after a fixed time is a SIGTERM from outside, not a crash. The kubelet log says it's acting on a failed liveness probe.

choices.text: Hunt for slow disk or network on the VM
choices.why: Reasonable for etcd in general, but nothing here points at I/O, and the regular two-minute rhythm points elsewhere.

choices.text: Fix the worker that runs an older Kubernetes version first
choices.why: A real side finding that day, worth fixing later. It doesn't explain the master's etcd dying.

steps.situation: The probe in the static pod manifest runs a test read against etcd.
steps.evidence:
$ grep -A9 livenessProbe /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml
    livenessProbe:
      exec:
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-ec", "ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl ... get foo"]
      failureThreshold: 8
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      timeoutSeconds: 15

choices.text: Copy the manifest outside the manifests folder, then remove or relax the probe in place
choices.why: The kubelet watches that folder and restarts etcd with the new spec. Eight failures of 15 seconds is about two minutes, the exact lifetime you saw. The backup must live elsewhere, or the kubelet runs it too.

choices.text: `kubectl edit pod etcd-master` to drop the probe
choices.why: That's a mirror pod. Static pods are defined by the file on disk; edits through the API don't stick.

choices.text: Wipe etcd's data directory so it starts clean
choices.why: etcd was healthy. You'd delete the whole cluster state to fix a probe.

debrief.what_happened: On 4 December 2018 NRE Labs went down. It ran on a single-master kubeadm cluster on one GCE VM, with etcd as a static pod, and `kubectl` got connection refused on port 6443. etcd and kube-apiserver had each restarted 183 times and the controller manager 91 times, which a check for Running status had missed. Restarting the kubelet helped briefly, and a fix was announced on Twitter too early. A worker on v1.11.3, against v1.12.x elsewhere, turned out to be a playbook error, and a full `terraform destroy` and rebuild of about 30 minutes brought the same failure back. `docker ps -a` then showed each etcd serving for 1.5 to 2 minutes before a SIGTERM: the kubelet was restarting it because the liveness probe (`etcdctl get foo`, timeout 15 s, failureThreshold 8) kept failing. Removing the probe from the manifest fixed it. Why the probe failed stayed open, since the same command succeeded by hand. The post's lessons: monitor a single master, keep a maintenance page, and check the basics before drastic action.
lessons: Read restart counts and container lifetimes, not just STATUS.
A regular kill interval points at a probe or a timer, not a crash.
Static pods live in /etc/kubernetes/manifests; keep backups outside it.
Don't rebuild or announce "fixed" before you know the cause.
